---
title: "Computational model of aesthetics"
description: "Aesthetic preferences as a policy for sampling perceptual-prior gradients."
---

::: {#key-ideas .callout-note title="Key ideas"}
- Aesthetic preferences may arise from optimizing how an agent moves and directs attention to collect samples for learning a perceptual prior.
- The extrinsic task policy determines which latents the prior should predict. The intrinsic policy determines which trajectories the agent samples to estimate the gradient of that prediction loss.
- The primary candidate uses vanilla behavioral policy optimization (BPO): it fits the intrinsic policy to a trajectory distribution that favors large gradients of the total latent negative log-likelihood.
:::

## What counts as a preference?

An agent looking at a painting can return its gaze to a detail or move on.
Both choices affect what it sees next. The hypothesis is that a repeatable
preference for one choice over the other can emerge from training the policy
that collects experience for perceptual learning. The model is about choices:
it does not require a stimulus to carry a beauty score or the agent to register
how much it learned after each glance.

In the [partially observable environment](pomdp-rl.qmd), a fixed
[perceptual encoder](perceptual-representations.qmd) maps input $x_t$ to a
latent $z_t$. Both policies select movement and attention using $z_t$ and a
memory $h_t$ of earlier experience. Their roles differ: the extrinsic policy
$\pi_e$ pursues task return, while the intrinsic policy $\pi_i$ collects
experience for estimating what the prior should learn under $\pi_e$.

The [efficient encoding account](perceptual-representations.qmd#efficient-encoding)
motivates fitting a normalized prior $R_\theta(z)$ to the encoder's outputs.
Here the target is the distribution of latents encountered during the task.
Sampling with $\pi_i$ changes how the prior gradient is estimated, not which
distribution the prior is meant to fit.

## Primary candidate: BPO over trajectories

Let $P_e$ and $P_i$ denote the trajectory laws of the two policies, with the
same horizon, initial conditions, and environment. For a realized trajectory
$\tau$ with latent sequence $z_{1:T}$, define
$$
L_\theta(\tau)=-\sum_{t=1}^T\log R_\theta(z_t),\qquad
G_\theta(\tau)=\nabla_\theta L_\theta(\tau).
$$
The prior scores each latent without conditioning on history; the samples
need not be independent. Differentiate with respect to the **prior parameters**,
holding the trajectory fixed. Add the gradient vectors before taking their
norm: two glances can each produce a large gradient yet largely cancel in the
trajectory total.

The target is $\mathbb E_{P_e}G_\theta$. A trajectory sampled under $\pi_i$
contributes $(P_e(\tau)/P_i(\tau))G_\theta(\tau)$ to its estimate. For shared
environment dynamics and memory updates the ratio is the product of the target
to sampling policy action-probability ratios along the trajectory. The estimate
is unbiased if the sampling policy covers all contributing target trajectories
and the expectation exists.

[Vanilla BPO](behavioral-policy-optimization.qmd) [@papini2024] fits a policy
to the variance-optimal importance proposal. Here the vector being estimated
is the prior gradient rather than a task-return policy gradient. Holding
$\theta$ and $\pi_e$ fixed for the fit, the proposal and policy objective are
$$
Q_\theta^*(\tau)=
\frac{P_e(\tau)\|G_\theta(\tau)\|_2}{\mathbb E_{P_e}\|G_\theta\|_2},
\qquad
\min_\phi D_{\rm KL}\!\left(Q_\theta^*\Vert P_{\pi_{i,\phi}}\right).
$$
For a finite, nonzero normalizer and finite second moments, the unrestricted
proposal minimizes the sum of the component variances. The **forward** KL fit
has the equivalent weighted log-likelihood objective
$$
\max_\phi\;
\mathbb E_{\tau\sim P_e}\!\left[
  \|G_\theta(\tau)\|_2
  \sum_{t=1}^{T}\log \pi_{i,\phi}(a_t\mid z_t,h_t)
\right].
$$
The intrinsic policy scores the actions taken by the target policy; one
gradient norm weights the entire sequence. The proposal normalizer and the
environment likelihood terms do not depend on $\phi$, so neither affects the
maximizer. This trains the intrinsic policy
parameters $\phi$; the importance-weighted gradient above trains $\theta$.
An action policy cannot in general realize an arbitrary trajectory law, so
the fit does not guarantee the unrestricted optimum.

An alternative [reverse-KL model](aesthetics-reverse-kl.qmd) fits the
distribution of individual latents instead. It gives each observed latent an
intrinsic reward; neither that reward nor its density-ratio estimator is
required by trajectory BPO.

## Testing the hypothesis

With the encoder, target policy, and prior checkpoint held fixed, one can ask
whether the fitted intrinsic policy reduces the variance of the target gradient
estimate relative to collecting the same number of task trajectories. A
separate behavioral test is whether its predicted gaze choices match observed
preferences. Success on the sampling test alone would not establish the
aesthetic hypothesis.
